fields.title: The Letter of Jude
fields.subtitle: Iouda, “Of Jude”
fields.description: A short, urgent letter from Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James, who meant to write about the salvation all believers share and wrote instead to urge his readers to fight hard for the faith handed over once for all. Intruders have slipped in who twist God’s grace into an excuse for shameless living: reefs hidden under the water, clouds that bring no rain, wandering stars. Cain, Balaam and Korah, Michael and the devil, Enoch’s prophecy; then the call to build, pray, keep yourselves in God’s love and show mercy, and the great doxology to the one who is able to guard you from stumbling. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Greek given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the letter’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: Who wrote the Letter of Jude, and when?
qa.answer: The writer calls himself “a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James” (1:1). The James meant is almost certainly James of Jerusalem, the brother of Jesus, which would make Jude another of Jesus’s brothers, named in Mark 6:3. Most who accept the letter as his date it between the 50s and 80s of the first century; some scholars think it was written later in his name. Its date and first readers are not stated.

qa.question: What is the Letter of Jude about?
qa.answer: Jude warns a church about people who “have slipped in among you without being noticed” and “twist our God’s grace into an excuse for shameless living” (1:4). He urges his readers to fight hard for “the faith that was handed over to God’s holy people once for all” (1:3), recalls examples of judgment from Israel’s history, and describes the intruders in vivid images. Then he tells his readers to build themselves up, pray in the Holy Spirit, keep themselves in God’s love and show mercy, and ends with a doxology to the God who is able to keep them from stumbling.

qa.question: Why does Jude quote the book of Enoch and tell the story of Michael and the body of Moses?
qa.answer: Verses 14–15 closely match a passage in 1 Enoch, a Jewish writing well known in the first century, and Origen says the story of Michael disputing with the devil over Moses’s body (1:9) comes from a book called the Ascension of Moses. Jude uses writings his readers knew to make his point. Some early Christians hesitated over the letter because of this, but most have understood that quoting a book does not make it Scripture, as Paul quoted Greek poets.

qa.question: Why does Jude mention Cain, Balaam and Korah?
qa.answer: “Woe to them! They have walked in the way of Cain. For the sake of pay they have thrown themselves into the error of Balaam. They have perished in the rebellion of Korah” (1:11). All three come from the Old Testament. Cain killed his brother; Balaam, the prophet hired to curse Israel, became a byword for doing wrong for money; Korah rose up against Moses and Aaron and was swallowed by the earth. Jude uses them as portraits of the intruders, who live by their own desires, serve for pay and “reject the Lord’s authority” (1:8). They join the letter’s earlier examples of judgment: Israel in the wilderness, the angels who did not stay in their place, and Sodom and Gomorrah (1:5–7).

qa.question: What is the doxology at the end of Jude?
qa.answer: The letter closes with one of the best-loved blessings in the New Testament: “Now to the one who is able to guard you from stumbling, and to bring you into the presence of his glory without blemish and rejoicing greatly, to God alone, our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, might, and authority, before time began, now, and for all the ages to come. Amen” (1:24–25). After a letter full of warnings, Jude ends not with his readers’ effort but with God’s. They are to keep themselves within God’s love (1:21), but it is God who guards them from stumbling. Churches have long used these words to close their worship.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. In verse 5, where manuscripts differ, it reads that “Jesus saved a people out of the land of Egypt”. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Greek beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
Dear friends, I was doing all I could to write to you about the salvation we hold in common, but I found I had to write and urge you to fight hard for the faith that was handed over to God’s holy people once for all.

— Jude 1:3

Jude meant to write a different letter. He tells us so in his first lines: he was doing all he could to write about “the salvation we hold in common”, the joyful things all believers share. But news reached him that changed his plans, and he wrote this instead, a short, urgent, fiery warning, crowded with images and with names from Israel’s past.

It is one of the least read books of the New Testament, and one of the most often quoted. Many people who could not find it in their Bibles know its last two verses by heart, because churches have sung and spoken them as a blessing for centuries. Between the warning and the blessing lies a letter that is far richer than its size, and far more hopeful than its reputation.

A servant, and a brother

The writer introduces himself as “a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James”. Only one James in the early church needed no further description: James of Jerusalem, the brother of Jesus. The Gospels name Judas (in English, Jude) among Jesus’s brothers as well (Mark 6:3). So the writer of this letter grew up in the same house as Jesus, and yet he does not call himself the Lord’s brother. He calls himself his servant. That is a quiet act of faith, and of humility.

We know almost nothing else about him. The historian Eusebius preserves a story, from the second-century writer Hegesippus, that the Emperor Domitian once had Jude’s grandsons brought before him because they were descendants of David, and let them go when he saw their calloused farmers’ hands. Some scholars think the letter was written later by someone in Jude’s circle, using his name; most who accept it as his date it somewhere between the 50s and the 80s of the first century. It may have been written to Jewish Christians, who would know every story it alludes to.

Why he wrote

Some people, Jude says, “have slipped in among you without being noticed” (1:4). He describes them as “ungodly people who twist our God’s grace into an excuse for shameless living, and who disown Jesus Christ, our only Master and Lord.” They were not outsiders attacking the church but insiders eating at its table, and their error was moral as much as doctrinal. They took the freedom of grace and made it a licence. They claimed visions and spiritual insight, rejected authority, and grumbled and flattered their way to what they wanted.

So Jude calls his readers to “fight hard for the faith that was handed over to God’s holy people once for all.” The faith, in this sentence, is not our act of believing but what is believed: the message about Jesus, given once and not to be revised.

Three warnings from the past

Jude reminds his readers of things they already know (1:5–7). God saved a people out of Egypt and afterward destroyed those who did not believe. Angels who abandoned their proper place are kept for judgment. Sodom and Gomorrah lie before us as an example. Each of the three had been richly blessed and turned from it, and each stands as a warning that privilege is not the same as faithfulness.

Later he names three more, in a single cry of woe:

Woe to them! They have walked in the way of Cain. For the sake of pay they have thrown themselves into the error of Balaam. They have perished in the rebellion of Korah.

— Jude 1:11

Cain, the jealous brother; Balaam, the prophet who could be bought; Korah, who rebelled against the leaders God had given. Jude says the intruders have done all three, and he writes as though their fate were already sealed.

Reefs, clouds, trees, waves, stars

Then comes a burst of pictures from the natural world, among the most vivid in the Bible (1:12–13). The intruders are “like reefs hidden under the water” at the church’s love feasts, waiting to wreck the unwary. They are “clouds that bring no rain”, promising much and giving nothing; “trees in late autumn with no fruit, twice dead and pulled up by the roots”; “wild waves of the sea, churning up their shameful deeds like foam”; “wandering stars”, which cannot be steered by. The images sweep across sea, sky and land. Wherever you look, there is something that seems to promise life and cannot give it.

Michael and Enoch

Two verses in Jude have puzzled readers more than any others. In verse 9 he tells how Michael the archangel, disputing with the devil over the body of Moses, did not dare to slander him, but said only, “May the Lord rebuke you.” The story is not in the Old Testament. Origen, early in the third century, says it comes from a book called the Ascension of Moses, which has not survived complete.

In verses 14–15 Jude quotes “Enoch, the seventh in line from Adam”, with words that closely match a passage in the book now called 1 Enoch, a Jewish writing well known in Jude’s day. Some in the early church, Jerome tells us, hesitated over Jude because of the quotation from Enoch; Eusebius lists it among the books disputed by some, though recognised by many. Christians have generally understood that quoting a book does not make it Scripture, any more than Paul made the Greek poets Scripture by quoting them. Jude uses stories his readers knew and honoured to make a point the whole Bible makes: God judges the ungodly, and humility, not slander, is the way of those who belong to him.

But you, dear friends

The turn comes in verse 17, with the words “But you, dear friends”. Jude has spent enough time on the intruders. Now he tells his readers what to do, and it is not to argue, but to build, pray, keep and wait:

But you, dear friends, keep building yourselves up on your most holy faith and praying in the Holy Spirit. Keep yourselves within God’s love, while you look forward to the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ that brings eternal life.

— Jude 1:20–21

And they are to show mercy, even to those who have been led astray. “Be merciful to some who are wavering. Save others by pulling them out of the fire.” The fight for the faith is not a fight against the people who are going wrong. It is a fight for them.

Kept

One word ties the letter together. Jude writes to those who are “kept safe for Jesus Christ” (1:1). The rebel angels did not keep their place, and are kept for judgment (1:6); the blackest darkness has been kept for the wandering stars (1:13). And the readers are told, “Keep yourselves within God’s love” (1:21). Then, in the final blessing, the one who keeps is God himself, “the one who is able to guard you from stumbling” (1:24). We are to keep ourselves in his love; but it is he who keeps us.

How to read Jude

Read it with the Old Testament stories it names in mind, and with 2 Peter 2 beside it. The two passages share much of their material, and most scholars think 2 Peter drew on Jude, though some think the reverse, or that both drew on a common source. Notice the letter’s threes: mercy, peace and love; three warnings, three villains, three kinds of mercy. Notice how much of it is spent on hope. And do not skip to the doxology too quickly. It shines brightest at the end of the dark letter that leads to it.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few of its choices in Jude are worth knowing about.

“Jesus saved a people.” In verse 5 the manuscripts differ more than anywhere else in the letter, between “Jesus”, “the Lord” and “God”. This translation reads “Jesus”, the harder reading and that of some important early manuscripts, so that Jude speaks of Jesus as the one who brought Israel out of Egypt.

“Reefs hidden under the water.” In verse 12, where older Bibles say “spots”, this translation reads the Greek word as hidden rocks, a danger to ships.

“Fight hard for the faith.” In verse 3, where older Bibles say “earnestly contend”, it uses plain words for a strenuous struggle. And where the Greek says “Christ”, the Open Word Bible lets a reader choose “Christ” or “the Messiah”; this edition prints “Christ”.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Greek beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: Jude 1
fields.body_html:
Greeting

From Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James, to those who have been called, who are loved by God the Father and kept safe for Jesus Christ. May mercy, peace, and love be yours in ever greater measure.

Fight for the faith

Dear friends, I was doing all I could to write to you about the salvation we hold in common, but I found I had to write and urge you to fight hard for the faith that was handed over to God’s holy people once for all. For some people have slipped in among you without being noticed. Long ago it was written that they would face this judgment. They are ungodly people who twist our God’s grace into an excuse for shameless living, and who disown Jesus Christ, our only Master and Lord.

Warnings from the past

Now I want to remind you of something, though you know it all already. Jesus saved a people out of the land of Egypt, but afterward he destroyed those among them who did not believe. And the angels who did not stay in the place of authority that was theirs, but abandoned their own dwelling, he has kept in everlasting chains in deepest darkness, ready for judgment when the great day comes. So too Sodom and Gomorrah and the towns around them, which, like those angels, gave themselves to sexual immorality and went after flesh of another kind, now lie before us as an example, suffering the penalty of eternal fire.

What these dreamers are like

Yet in the same way these dreamers defile their bodies, reject the Lord’s authority, and slander the glorious ones. But when Michael, the archangel, was in a dispute with the devil, arguing over the body of Moses, he did not dare to bring a slanderous judgment against him. Instead he said, “May the Lord rebuke you.” But these people slander what they know nothing about, while the things they know by instinct, like animals without reason, are the very things that destroy them. Woe to them! They have walked in the way of Cain. For the sake of pay they have thrown themselves into the error of Balaam. They have perished in the rebellion of Korah. At your love feasts these people are like reefs hidden under the water. They eat with you without a trace of fear, shepherds who look after only themselves. They are clouds that bring no rain, blown along by the winds; trees in late autumn with no fruit, twice dead and pulled up by the roots; wild waves of the sea, churning up their shameful deeds like foam; wandering stars, for whom the blackest darkness has been kept forever.

Enoch’s prophecy

Enoch, the seventh in line from Adam, also prophesied about these people. He said, “Look! The Lord is coming with tens of thousands of his holy ones to bring judgment on everyone, and to prove all the ungodly guilty of every ungodly deed they have done in their ungodliness, and of every hard word spoken against him by ungodly sinners.” These people grumble and find fault with their lot in life. They live by their own desires. Their mouths speak big, boastful words, and they flatter people to get something out of them.

Keep yourselves in God’s love

But you, dear friends, must remember the words spoken in advance by the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ. They used to tell you, “In the last time, scoffers will come, driven by their own ungodly desires.” These people create divisions among you. They are worldly, and the Spirit is not in them. But you, dear friends, keep building yourselves up on your most holy faith and praying in the Holy Spirit. Keep yourselves within God’s love, while you look forward to the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ that brings eternal life. Be merciful to some who are wavering. Save others by pulling them out of the fire. To still others show mercy, but with fear: hate even the clothes their sinful flesh has soiled.

Praise to the God who guards you

Now to the one who is able to guard you from stumbling, and to bring you into the presence of his glory without blemish and rejoicing greatly, to God alone, our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, might, and authority, before time began, now, and for all the ages to come. Amen.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
Now to the one who is able to guard you from stumbling, and to bring you into the presence of his glory without blemish and rejoicing greatly, to God alone, our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, might, and authority, before time began, now, and for all the ages to come. Amen.

— Jude 1:24–25

No letter in the New Testament ends more gloriously than this one, and none has a darker road leading up to it. Jude has written of intruders, judgment, fire and the blackest darkness. Then, in one long sentence, he lifts his readers’ eyes from all of it to God, who is able to bring them safely home and set them, without blemish and rejoicing, in the presence of his glory.

The question the book leaves with you

Jude asks whether we will hold on to the faith once handed over, or let it be quietly reshaped into something more comfortable. The intruders did not announce that they were abandoning Christ. They simply turned grace into an excuse, and went on eating at the love feasts. Jude’s warning is that this can happen to any church, without anyone noticing, unless someone cares enough to say so.

But the letter’s deeper question is where our confidence rests. Jude tells his readers to keep themselves in God’s love, and he means it. Yet he does not end by telling them to be strong. He ends by telling them who is strong. The faith is worth fighting for because God is able to keep those who hold it.

Where to go from here

Jude has been less preached than almost any book of the Bible, but its best verses run through the church’s classics, and several are in this library:

  • On the faith handed over (1:3). J. C. Ryle’s Knots Untied, whose papers on “divers and strange doctrines” and on the fallibility of ministers take Jude’s call to contend for the faith as a plain Christian duty.
  • On praying in the Holy Spirit (1:20). R. A. Torrey’s The Person and Work of the Holy Spirit, which calls this verse one of the most deeply significant in the Bible on prayer, and the reading for October 8 in Charles H. Spurgeon’s Evening by Evening.
  • On the one who is able to keep you (1:24). Spurgeon’s reading for October 9 in Morning by Morning.
  • On the man and his letter. Eusebius of Caesarea’s The Church History, which tells the story of Jude’s grandsons before Domitian and how the letter was received; and Origen’s On First Principles, which names the book behind the story of Michael and the body of Moses.
  • On the teachers Jude warned against. Irenaeus of Lyons’s Against Heresies, which describes a later sect that honoured Cain, Korah and the people of Sodom, the very names Jude holds up as warnings.

But the best next step may be to learn the doxology by heart. Christians have spoken it over one another for nearly two thousand years, at the end of services and at partings. Say it slowly, and let each phrase land: able to guard you; without blemish; rejoicing greatly; to God alone. Then go back to the beginning of the letter, and hear how Jude greeted his readers before he said anything else:

May mercy, peace, and love be yours in ever greater measure.

— Jude 1:2
